title: Making a bad thing worse
core: All three take a situation that is *already* bad and describe it getting worse — none of them can start from a neutral baseline. Where they split is the *mechanism* of worsening: whether something new was added on top, whether the existing trouble simply got more severe, or whether it climbed to a higher level in stages. That mechanism also determines who or what gets blamed, and how formal the sentence sounds.

words.nuance: **Compound** requires a *second, separate act* layered on the first — the crash, then the lie about it. That extra act is usually a choice, so the verb quietly assigns blame in a way the other two don't; it also carries the compound-interest sense of damage feeding on itself. Watch the decoys: its literal senses (a mixture, a walled compound, a compound fracture) have nothing to do with worsening.

**Exacerbate** adds no new element and no stages — the same problem simply becomes more severe or inflamed. It prefers an impersonal subject (a policy, a drought, a remark exacerbates; a person rarely does) and an object that is already a named ailment: a shortage, a deficit, tensions, an injury. This is the formal one — the verb of medical charts and policy reports.

**Escalate** is the only one with rungs: it moves things up by stages into a different league — skirmish to war, quarrel to brawl — and each step provokes the next, so it happily runs intransitively with no agent at all (*the conflict escalated*). Note the change of kind, not just degree. Its office sense — passing a matter up to a higher authority — is neutral, even helpful.

exam_note: The trap is mechanism-blindness: sentences that supply a distinct second act want **compound**, ones describing a step up in kind want **escalate**, and only **exacerbate** fits when nothing new happens but an existing condition intensifies — plus the neutral "escalate to my manager" sense is fair game.
